title: The Guru as light
hook: one of his saloks says all is darkness without the Guru

segments.voice: Yesterday, the quiet successor's words: Guru Angad's saloks, see without eyes, walk without feet. Your line was few words, deep. Did you say one thing today with fewer words than usual? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.

A snowfield at midday. Light pours down from the sky and bounces back up off the snow until everything is one bright white. You can see perfectly well. The trail markers are buried, and you have no idea which way the path goes. Plenty of light. No direction. The light that fills your eyes and the light that shows you the way are not the same thing. Guru Angad has a salok built on exactly that difference, and the picture is enormous. Today: what kind of light he means.
screen: `A SNOWFIELD AT MIDDAY.` → `PLENTY OF LIGHT.` → `NO DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: The salok sits in Asa di Var, the ballad sung in the morning at the gurdwara, and it's marked Mahala two. Here it is, in paraphrase. If a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns appeared, even with all that light, without the Guru there would be pitch darkness. Stop on the size of that picture. A hundred moons. A thousand suns. He piles up more light than any sky has ever held, and then says it isn't enough. So he can't mean light for the eyes. He means the light that shows a person where they are and which way to go: what's true, what's ego, what's worth a life. In Sikh teaching, that light comes from the Guru. And who is the Guru? For Sikhs, the Gurus in their lifetimes, and now the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word itself. Earlier this year, in the Sidh Gosht, we heard Guru Nanak say the Word is the Guru. Guru Angad's salok shows what that Guru does. It doesn't add more brightness to a world already full of it. It turns darkness of a different kind into sight. Notice, too, how the salok works on the listener. It's easy to assume more is the answer: more information, more options, more light on the screen. This verse quietly says no. You can be flooded with light and still be in the dark. What changes things isn't how much you can see, but whether something guides your seeing. That's today's line.
screen: `A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.` · `STILL, PITCH DARKNESS.` · `THE LIGHT THAT SHOWS THE WAY.` · `NOT MORE LIGHT, BUT GUIDED SIGHT.` · then, large: `THE GURU AS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your light. In the sit, let the breath slow. Remember a time you had plenty of information and still didn't know which way to go. Then remember what helped you see: a teacher, a line from a text, a parent, a friend, a hard lesson. Let that one come clearly to mind. Hold it with thanks for a few slow breaths. If you pray, you can thank the Guru, and say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The Guru as light. Guru Angad's picture: a hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru, the light that shows the way. Today's word.
Your line: the guru as light. The next time you're stuck, before reaching for more information, ask what would show you the way. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok when Asa di Var is sung in the morning at the gurdwara, and Sikh teachers use it to speak of the Guru's guidance, through the Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib.
